claims.text: The United States moved to force TikTok’s sale or ban it primarily due to national-security concerns regarding the potential for Chinese government access to U.S. [Source: ev-1]
user data and the platform's algorithm [Source: ev-1].

This concern was formalized through CFIUS review and led to the passage of the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, which President Biden signed on 2024-04-24 [Source: ev-1].
The law required ByteDance to divest TikTok’s U.S. [Source: ev-1]
operations within roughly 270 days (extendable by 90) or face a ban in the United States [Source: ev-1].

The dispute progressed as follows:
*   On 2025-01-17, one day before the effective date of 2025-06-19, the Supreme Court upheld the law with a unanimous 9-0 per curiam decision [Source: ev-1].
*   Consequently, TikTok went dark in the US on 2025-04-18/19 for approximately 14 hours [Source: ev-1].
*   The app was restored on 2025-4-19 after President Trump pledged to pause enforcement; his executive order dated 2025-6-20 delayed enforcement for another 75 days [Source: ev-1].
The dispute was ultimately resolved through an Oracle-led deal announced on 2025-. [Source: ev-1]
This resolution structured TikTok’s U.S. [Source: ev-1]
operations as a joint venture rather than an outright sale, ensuring that the app stayed live under "Project Texas," which hosted US user data in Oracle's cloud under US control [Source: ev-1].
Under this agreement, ByteDance retained a majority interest, while Oracle received about a 12.5% stake in TikTok's U.S. [Source: ev-1]
operations, with participation from SoftBank and other investors [Source: ev-1].
Vice President JD Vance led the White House negotiations for this final ownership structure, which was completed through 2025 [Source: ev-1].
